name: Bianca Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, governments or political parties. We don’t sell anything or campaign, and your answers are confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Most mornings I read the customer cases nobody else could settle, then sit with one of my twelve complaint officers and work through what went wrong. This is a large household goods company, and I lead the regional complaints team; I'm 43, have an MBA and get typical pay, not director money. My partner maintains school grounds, our children are ten and twelve, and we have a mortgage and 20,000 saved against monthly spending of 5,000. I've never used an AI tool, and I still take handwritten notes because a crossed-out promise tells me something a neat summary doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're allowed to get on with the work now. Customers have been hearing for years that a machine will sort everything out, and then somebody like my officer Mara has to explain a missing refund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel that my job and our household money were reasonably secure. My 4,700 take-home and my partner's 1,500 cover the 5,000 budget, and the 20,000 reserve is separate from the small monthly amounts set aside for annual bills. I'd be quietly pleased that refusing to rush into AI hadn't cost me my place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep our Thursday case review and the handwritten promise log through the first year. I'd continue the existing transfer of our 1,200 monthly surplus to savings, without starting a new course or changing the mortgage plan. If someone offered me an AI writing tool, I'd leave it alone and keep writing my own replies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and slightly vindicated, though I wouldn't put the second part in a staff email. A familiar week can be a very good week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the Thursday review worth keeping?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week a trainee spotted that a customer had been promised collection twice, and the dates were in two different files. Sitting together got the promise honoured; I wouldn't throw that habit away because the work looked untidy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell your team you felt vindicated?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, because two of the younger officers like the tools and I don't want a little victory parade at their expense. I'd say the quality of the reply matters, and leave my private satisfaction out of it.

say: I'd say we can **get on** with resolving customer complaints and explaining missing refunds.
I'd tell the team that **reply quality** matters without mocking colleagues who like new tools.
think: I consider my **job and household** money reasonably secure with two wages and a separate reserve.
I feel privately **vindicated** that avoiding AI hasn't cost me my place at work.
do: Keep the **Thursday review** and handwritten promise log throughout the first year.
Continue the existing **1,200 monthly** savings transfer without changing the mortgage plan or taking a course.
feel: **Calm and vindicated**, with a preference for familiar weeks.
S0.quote: A familiar week can be a very good week.
fieldNote: Her **calm** rests on a current surplus and four months of expenses saved, rather than a general dislike of change.
She keeps **private satisfaction** separate from her public treatment of younger officers who favour the tools.

steps.text: Continue Thursday complaint reviews and the handwritten promise log
Continue transferring the existing 1,200 monthly surplus to savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody should be judged by the speed of a draft alone. If AI writes and checks most replies, the company needs to say openly what happens to the people who used to do that work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think our team was a clear place to cut because writing, checking and assigning cases fill most of our week. My own case knowledge wouldn't stop the company deciding it needed fewer managers. I could lose my salary, and I'd hate having to admit that after telling everyone to be patient.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'd ask our staff association to include my grade in its staffing questions, not just the officers. In the first year of change I'd attend the monthly evening members' meeting and ask for published selection rules and notice periods before any reductions. I'd also ask the three nearby large employers I know about their current complaints vacancies, but I wouldn't resign without a signed offer at no less than my current 4,700 take-home. Those enquiries aren't offers, and I wouldn't privately feed customer cases into AI to try to impress an interviewer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, especially about being responsible for other people's confidence while mine shrinks. I feel cross as well, because refusing a writing tool shouldn't mean accepting a secret staffing decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you actually learn the tool if it became compulsory?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd first ask for a person to show me exactly what was required and what customer information could go into it. I haven't agreed to use it in this picture; I'd probably put that conversation off, even though I can see that delay might damage my chances.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a local move solve the problem?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the other complaints teams would face the same pressure. I'd still ask because a real opening could buy some time, but I wouldn't describe the move to my partner as a safe new career.

say: I'd demand open answers about **staffing** when software takes over writing and checking replies.
I'd say **draft speed** alone is a poor measure of complaint work.
think: I think both my **team and job** are exposed because writing, checking and assigning cases dominate our week.
I dread admitting **my own risk** after asking colleagues to remain patient.
do: Ask the **staff association** to cover managers and attend monthly evening meetings seeking written selection and notice rules.
Enquire at **three local employers**; resign only after a signed offer provides at least 4,700 take-home.
feel: **Anxious and cross**, with responsibility for colleagues adding to her worry.
S1.quote: My own case knowledge wouldn't stop the company deciding it needed fewer managers.
fieldNote: She recognises **management exposure**, while her refusal to experiment with AI may narrow her remaining options.
Her **local enquiries** have an explicit pay and offer gate, and she does not treat another complaints job as protection.

steps.text: Attend staff association meetings and request written staffing rules covering managers
Ask three local employers about complaints vacancies before considering any signed offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the company can't describe a whole department losing its living as a personal training failure. I'd ask for a joint meeting about leaving terms, because a pile of separate emails would let the same question go unanswered twelve times.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd expect to lose my job around 2028, and another complaints desk wouldn't be a way out if almost any thinking work could be done cheaply. My partner's 1,500 wouldn't carry a 5,000 budget. Our 20,000 reserve is four months of full costs, not four years to become somebody else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take my own contract and household budget to the staff association adviser now and ask what notice and leaving payments actually apply; I wouldn't copy customer files. I'd remove the 600 monthly holiday allocation and 400 of optional shopping, bringing spending to 4,000, and keep the existing reserve available. If I lost my pay in the first year after AGI, I'd ask the mortgage lender about a temporary reduction before missing a payment and apply for whatever income support I was actually eligible for. Without support or leaving money, the 2,500 gap after my partner's wage would use today's 20,000 in eight months; I'd ask about selling the house before that point, not count on a payment arriving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, with an urge to keep checking the bank even though checking doesn't add anything. I wouldn't be rushing happily into a new occupation; I'd be trying to keep a sequence of bad decisions from starting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the later arrival of robots reassure you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only about my partner's work for a while, and even that isn't a promise from the school. My complaints work is thinking work, so the 2031 robots don't give my salary three extra years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept any retraining place that was offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to know the fees, the hours and whether there were paid jobs at the end, and I might still be slow to say yes. A free class doesn't pay a mortgage while you're in the classroom, and I won't put an unaccepted place in our income column.

say: I'd call for a **joint meeting** about leaving terms rather than blame individuals for a department's disappearance.
I'd insist that **training language** doesn't answer the question of how families live after job loss.
think: I expect my **job** to end around 2028 because another complaints desk faces the same thinking AI.
Our **20,000 reserve** is only four months of current costs, while my partner earns 1,500 monthly.
do: Bring my **contract and budget** to the association adviser to establish actual notice and leaving entitlements.
Remove **1,000 monthly** in holidays and shopping, preserving cash against a possible income gap.
Request **mortgage relief** and eligible support after job loss, checking a house sale before unsupported cash runs out.
feel: **Alarmed**, repeatedly checking the bank and fearing a chain of bad decisions.
S2.quote: Our 20,000 reserve is four months of full costs, not four years to become somebody else.
fieldNote: Her **eight-month calculation** uses today's reserve and reduced costs, excludes unconfirmed help and allows no imaginary replacement wage.
The **robot delay** may extend her partner's grounds work but does not extend her own desk salary.

steps.text: Ask the association adviser to establish her notice and leaving entitlements
Remove 600 in holiday saving and 400 in optional shopping monthly
Request mortgage relief and apply for eligible income support after salary loss

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the association we have time to ask for a proper transition agreement before the department is dismantled. I'd want ordinary staff and managers in the same room, because being made to compete for sympathy would waste those years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still expect my complaints salary to disappear around 2031, and I wouldn't suddenly become comfortable with new technology because the date moved. The extra years would let us make a choice about the house while we still had two incomes. I'm frightened of waiting until the savings dictate every choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd book two house valuations this winter and ask the lender what smaller mortgage we could actually obtain, including moving fees and any early repayment charge. My partner and I would look at smaller homes within the children's current school area; we'd move only if a completed sale and approved new loan left 20,000 accessible and cut monthly costs by at least 700 after all fees. Until then I'd continue our existing 1,200 monthly saving, without treating a valuation as cash. In the first year after AGI I'd use whatever reserve we'd actually built and meet the association adviser about job loss; I wouldn't assume we had moved or won a transition agreement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, though I can picture doing those appointments without falling apart. Having time to choose which cupboard to empty feels different from having the bank choose the moving date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about looking at smaller homes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them we were trying to keep their school and friends while making the bills easier to carry. I wouldn't promise a move until the money and the purchase were agreed, because a viewing isn't a new home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the extra years to learn AI instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People would certainly suggest it, and I'd probably keep saying I needed to finish the complaints first. That's a weakness in my plan, but I know myself; I can arrange a valuation sooner than I can make myself trust a generated answer.

say: I'd ask the **association** to seek a transition agreement before the department is dismantled.
I'd want **managers and staff** together rather than competing for sympathy.
think: I still expect my **complaints salary** to disappear around 2031, without becoming comfortable with new technology.
I fear **waiting too long** until depleted savings decide every household choice.
do: Book **two valuations**; consider homes within the children's school area, obtaining lending terms that include moving fees and repayment charges.
Move only after **completed sale** and approved loan preserve 20,000 accessible cash and cut monthly costs by at least 700 after fees.
Continue **1,200 monthly** saving until any move, then use actual reserves and association advice if the job ends.
feel: **Alarmed but able** to picture choosing and completing practical appointments.
S3.quote: I can arrange a valuation sooner than I can make myself trust a generated answer.
fieldNote: Her **housing plan** has sale, loan, cash and cost gates; neither a valuation nor a viewing becomes available money.
She admits **avoidance** of AI, so the longer runway creates household action rather than an implausibly rapid technical reinvention.

steps.text: Seek a staff association transition agreement covering staff and managers
Consider smaller homes within the children's school area under the sale, loan, cash and cost gates
Continue the existing 1,200 monthly saving until any completed move

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is enough time for employers and public authorities to stop pretending every household can solve this alone. I'd support an income bridge with published eligibility rules, including people whose jobs disappear before pension age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 53 when the thinking work goes, with children of twenty and twenty-two. I still expect to lose my salary, and my partner's grounds work could be exposed to robots around 2039, so neither of us has a guaranteed wage through retirement. Ten years makes the arithmetic less frightening, but I can't call myself retired just because the company stops paying me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask our lender now for a no-fee illustration of paying the mortgage down over ten years, while leaving our 20,000 emergency reserve untouched. I'd commit only if the required extra payment fitted inside the current 1,200 monthly surplus; otherwise I'd keep the existing payment and savings rather than promise a payoff. Over the preparation years I'd send my elected representative a request for a funded income bridge, and in the first year after AGI I'd apply only if such a scheme existed and I qualified. If my salary ended without it, we'd use actual savings and ask the lender for terms before missing payments, not assume the mortgage or our working years were finished.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still alarmed about the two wages in the long run, though I can talk about this picture without feeling cornered today. I'd rather have a mortgage statement to work on than another invitation to reinvent myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are you assuming an income bridge will exist?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, a letter from me isn't a law or a payment award. Until there's a funded scheme and an approval in my name, our budget gets zero from it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen to plans to help the children through further study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd discuss actual course and living costs with them before agreeing contributions. I'd explain that support from us has to fit beside our own bills, rather than promise ten years ahead that we can pay for everything.

say: I'd support a **funded income bridge** with published eligibility before pension age.
I'd say **employers and authorities** have responsibilities alongside household planning.
think: At **53**, I expect my salary to go, with my partner's grounds income also exposed later.
Ten years eases the **arithmetic**, but losing my job doesn't create a retirement income.
do: Request a **ten-year mortgage** illustration without spending the existing 20,000 reserve.
Make extra payments only within the **1,200 surplus**; otherwise continue existing payments and savings.
Write to my **elected representative**, applying for an income bridge only if a funded scheme exists and I qualify.
feel: **Alarmed about both wages**, though less cornered by immediate household choices.
S4.quote: I can't call myself retired just because the company stops paying me.
fieldNote: Her **mortgage payoff** remains conditional on a lender illustration and affordable payments; she never declares the loan cleared.
She gives **policy support** no budget value before a funded scheme and individual approval, despite strongly favouring collective provision.

steps.text: Request an affordable ten-year mortgage illustration while protecting the emergency reserve
Write to her elected representative requesting a funded income bridge
Apply for an income bridge only if funded eligibility rules permit

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd expect my whole sort of work to go before I've worked out what comes next. Written consultation rights, a clearly funded income bridge and a mortgage answer before the final payday would help; I don't have those promises now. I can read a difficult customer's letter without flinching, but I can't read my family's future off a course brochure.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the people who don't volunteer for every new system but still do careful work. I don't want my reluctance to use AI mistaken for reluctance to work. I've stayed late beside frightened junior staff often enough to know those are different things.

headlineQuote: I don't want my reluctance to use AI mistaken for reluctance to work.
portrait: Bianca is **43**, a respected MBA manager leading twelve complaint officers at a large household goods company.
She has **two children**, a mortgage, a groundskeeper partner and four months of current household expenses saved.
She has **never used AI** and relies on handwritten case notes, established procedures and careful attention to junior staff.
She seeks **collective protections** and household choices across the scenarios, without assuming another office job survives AGI.
biggestWorry: I fear **AGI by 2028** most because my entire field could disappear before I find a next step.
whatWouldHelp: I need **consultation rights**, a funded income bridge and a mortgage answer before my last payday.
